opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's useful to look at it historically. From roughly 2012 to 2020, that was an age of research. People were trying lots of different ideas and seeing what worked. Then, around 2020 to 2025, it became an age of scaling. The word "scaling" itself was very powerful, because it told people what to do. You had a recipe: take more compute, more data, a bigger neural net, and you get better results. Companies loved that, because it's a very low-risk way to invest resources. You know that if you put more in, you'll get something out.

But the recipe has limits. Pre-training data is finite. We can see where that ends. Compute has grown enormously, so the question becomes: if you had a hundred times more, would everything be transformed? I don't think so. It would make a difference, but I don't believe it would be the kind of difference where you just turn the crank and arrive somewhere fundamentally new.

So we're back to needing ideas. The difference is that now we do research with very big computers. And there's an interesting point here: during the scaling era, scaling sucked the air out of the room. Everyone was doing the same thing, so there were more companies than ideas. Now the bottleneck shifts back toward ideas.

And I think the clearest sign we need new ideas is generalization. These models do incredibly well on evals, yet in practice they have strange failures. You ask a model to fix a bug, it introduces a second bug, you point that out, and it brings the first one back. Somehow the models generalize dramatically worse than people do. A teenager learns to drive in about ten hours. A person picks up a new skill with very little data and is robust about it. Understanding why, and what the underlying principle is, is a research question, not a scaling question. That's what I find most exciting about this moment.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training data is finite and identifies it as a limit.

r002.rationale: It doubts that 100 times more compute would produce a fundamentally new outcome by simply scaling up.

r003.rationale: It describes the return to research as doing research with very big computers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying that the age of scaling was a very unusual period. From maybe 2020 to 2025, the field had this remarkably clear recipe. You take a bigger neural network, you give it more data, you give it more compute, and it gets better. And everyone could see it. It was a very low-risk way of investing resources, which is why companies did it. If you have a recipe that works, the rational thing is to pour everything into the recipe.

But I think what people are now noticing is that the recipe is running into some kind of limit. Not a hard wall, exactly. It's more that the data is finite. The internet is finite. And pre-training on the internet, which was the main source of the scaling gains, is something you can only do so many times. You can scale the compute, but the thing that made scaling so productive was that compute and data grew together.

So what happens when that stops being the case? You go back to asking questions. What are these models actually missing? Why does a model that can do very impressive things on a benchmark still fail in ways that a person would not fail? Why is their generalization so much worse than human generalization, even though they have seen vastly more than any human? These are not questions you answer by making the model bigger. They are questions you answer by thinking, by trying ideas, by being wrong a lot.

And I'd say the other thing is that scaling, in a sense, hid how little we understood. When something works, you don't feel the need to understand it. Now that the easy gains are harder to come by, the understanding becomes the bottleneck again. And that's what research is. I actually find it quite exciting. For a while, the field was mostly engineering, in a very serious and impressive way, but engineering. Now it has to become science again.

r001.rationale: It says internet data is finite and that pre-training on it can only be repeated so many times.

r002.rationale: It argues that simply making models bigger will not answer key questions, but does not express the specific 100-times-scale claim.

r003.rationale: It describes a return to research and separately mentions scaling compute, but does not characterize the research itself as using very large computing resources.

astra-6.text:
I think the emphasis on scaling came from the fact that we had a recipe that worked remarkably well. You could take a fairly similar approach, make the model bigger, train it on more data, use more compute, and get better results. When that works, it makes sense to put a lot of effort into it.

But that recipe cannot continue unchanged forever. In particular, the amount of data available to us is finite. Compute can keep increasing, but you need to know what to do with it. You need a training procedure that turns that additional compute into additional capability.

And that is a research question. Can we make models learn more from the data they see? Can they discover things through interaction? Can they reliably improve through experience?

So I don’t think scaling goes away. I think the question shifts from “How much can we scale this recipe?” to “What is the next recipe worth scaling?”

r001.rationale: The response says the available data is finite and that the current scaling recipe cannot continue unchanged, identifying data as an eventual limit.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a 100-fold increase in training scale or express skepticism about that increase alone producing a transformative change.

r003.rationale: It connects research to using additional compute, but does not characterize the return to research as research conducted with very large computing resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to think about it is that scaling was a very particular recipe. You take a neural network, you make it bigger, you train it on more data, and it gets better. And because this worked so reliably, it made sense to put a tremendous amount of effort into doing it at larger scales.

But that recipe cannot continue unchanged forever. In particular, the amount of readily available data is finite. Compute can keep growing, but you need to figure out what useful work to do with that compute. Just making the same training run bigger is not a complete answer.

So you return to research. How should these systems learn? How do you get more learning out of the experience they have? How do you make their capabilities generalize more reliably? Those become central questions again.

It doesn’t mean scale stops mattering. It means that the thing you scale becomes more of an open question. And that’s a situation where a good idea can make a very large difference.

r001.rationale: The response says the amount of readily available data is finite and presents this as a limit on simply scaling the same training recipe.

r002.rationale: It questions whether simply making the same training run bigger is enough, but does not address a 100-fold increase or whether that alone would be transformative.

r003.rationale: The response says compute can keep growing and that research questions return, but does not characterize that research as being conducted with very large computing resources.
